maintopic: MR. LESSARD-C.B.C. INTERVIEWS WITH MEMBERS OF FLAG COMMITTEE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: MR. LESSARD-C.B.C. INTERVIEWS WITH MEMBERS OF FLAG COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege to denounce something that took place this morning which in my opinion was an insult not only to all the French Canadian members of the house but to all French Canadians in Canada.
During the press conference the special committee on the flag held this morning the journalists and the radio and television commentators were given the opportunity and the privilege of seeing an array of the flags the committee has received, and were able to ask questions to which, of course, they did not get the answers they had hoped for. They also questioned some individual members of the committee.
The C.B.C., a crown corporation, was represented, but its English speaking section only. On several occasions the technicians filmed a close-up of certain members of the committee, that is, four members out of five from the Conservative party, six members out of seven from the Liberal party, but no member from the splinter parties and, particularly, no French Canadian member, that is, five members out of five who sit on that committee.

maintopic: MR. LESSARD-C.B.C. INTERVIEWS WITH MEMBERS OF FLAG COMMITTEE
speechtext: Shame, shame.

maintopic: MR. LESSARD-C.B.C. INTERVIEWS WITH MEMBERS OF FLAG COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this shows how little respect the C.B.C. has for justice, and it confirms the opinion of several persons who claim that some degree of discrimination exists in that corporation.
Several members of this house voiced their consternation at what is happening at present in the province of Quebec, and concerning those demonstrations against confederation and the way the French Canadians are treated as such.
This instance, by itself, is insignificant. But when added to thousands of other similar instances which are more or less an insult to the French Canadian population of this country, it explains, I believe, why French Canadians are dissatisfied with confederation and the Anglo-Saxon group.
Being financed through public funds, a good deal of which are provided by French Canadians, the C.B.C. has a great responsibil-

ity in the present economic and social climate and that crown corporation is not true to its obligations in my opinion, when it fails to foresee circumstances like those of this morning.
I hope the Secretary of State, who answers to this house for that irresponsible organization, will see to it that there is no recurrence of such incidents; otherwise, certain acts will be doubly justified.

maintopic: MR. LESSARD-C.B.C. INTERVIEWS WITH MEMBERS OF FLAG COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say first of all that I do not agree with the hon. member when he suggests that the C.B.C. is discriminating against French Canadians.

maintopic: MR. LESSARD-C.B.C. INTERVIEWS WITH MEMBERS OF FLAG COMMITTEE
speechtext: It definitely is.

maintopic: MR. LESSARD-C.B.C. INTERVIEWS WITH MEMBERS OF FLAG COMMITTEE
speechtext: However, I can assure the hon. member that I will inquire about the reasons why representatives of the French network were not present at this morning's interviews.

maintopic: MR. LESSARD-C.B.C. INTERVIEWS WITH MEMBERS OF FLAG COMMITTEE
speechtext: That will not correct this morning's blunder, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: NATIONAL CONFERENCE ON TRAFFIC SAFETY
speechtext:
The Canadian highway safety council held its 10th annual conference on highway safety in May, 1964. These annual conferences are attended by leaders from insurance companies, oil, rubber and automotive industries. Persons concerned with safety programs in federal, provincial and municipal government departments also participate.
Assessment is made of traffic accident trends, and courses of action are planned. The proceedings are published listing the transactions of the various working committees.
The federal government, through the Department of National Health and Welfare, gives financial support to the Canadian highway safety council. Close liaison is maintained between Department of National Health and Welfare staff and the council. Under these circumstances no consideration is being given at the present time to calling under federal auspices any additional national conference to promote traffic safety.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: COVERAGE OF VISIT TO OTTAWA BY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
I direct this question to the Secretary of State, and ask him whether his attention has been drawn to an article appearing in the Globe and Mail this morning under the heading "CTV Scores Beat". It has to do with the broadcast of Her Majesty's arrival in Ottawa next Sunday and it states.

Supply-Justice
among other things, that the C.B.C. has shown a curious tendency to downgrade the Queen's activities.
Would the minister bring to the attention of the C.B.C. that because the corporation is not broadcasting the Queen's visit "live" on Sunday evening upon her arrival, the only people who will be able to see what is going on will be the 75 per cent who could use the private CTV facilities? Would the minister also bring to the attention of the C.B.C. the fact that Canadians everywhere want to see this visit of the Queen to Canada's capital, and there is no reason why there should not be a live showing rather than a postponed production?

subtopic: COVERAGE OF VISIT TO OTTAWA BY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: COVERAGE OF VISIT TO OTTAWA BY THE QUEEN
speechtext: I have not seen the article in question, but I will be pleased to convey to the C.B.C. the views of the right hon. gentleman.
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue.
Can he give the house the assurance that at the next federal-provincial conference on taxation, scheduled to take place on October 14 and 15 next, consideration will be given to means of cutting taxes instead of studying ways to increase them?

I am not certain whether the hon. member is serious. In any event, perhaps he would put his question on the order paper.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

Legal and other services-
1. Administration including the office of the superintendent of bankruptcy, grants and contributions as detailed in the estimates, gratuities to the widows or other dependants of judges who die while in office and authority to make recoverable advances for the administration of justice on behalf of the governments of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, $2,109,600.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The estimates of my department are being called today as a result of a procedure which was adopted in this chamber on Monday,

October 5, when the right hon. Leader of the Opposition moved the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a matter which, he alleged, was of urgent national interest, namely the way in which the present government has dealt with one Hal Banks.
I cannot refrain from making a special reference to the fact that such a motion should have been made on that particular date. It would be a refusal of duty on my part not to make a special note of the courtesy and the admirable sense of courage shown on that day by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition.
Oh, shame.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There were three members of the government who were likely to have to answer the very serious accusations which he made and intended to press on that day. These were the Prime Minister of Canada, the Minister of Labour and myself, in my capacity as Minister of Justice. It is interesting to note that this particular day was chosen when the Prime Minister was attending the ceremonies in connection with the arrival of the Queen in Charlottetown-
Do not be so cowardly.
Imputing motives.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am just stating facts; I am not imputing motives.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This was also a day when the Minister of Labour was attending the official opening of the British Columbia institute of technology and when I, for that day and the beginning of the following day, was chairing the conference of attorneys general sitting in the west block to try to arrive at a formula to provide for the amendment in Canada of the constitution of Canada.
You want to see what your pals did in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Let not the right hon. gentleman state that the matter in his opinion was urgent on that particular day, because on the preceding Friday he had gone a long way toward trying to make a great deal about the fact that a Toronto reporter was alleged to have spoken to Banks on a yacht in New York harbour. I wish to note this because I do not believe it would have been fair to press any of the accusations the right hon. Leader of the Opposition made on that day, at a time when it was known that neither the Prime Minister, nor the Minister of

Labour nor myself would be here to defend either ourselves, our respective departments or officers.
Or Banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Four charges or accusations were made against the government with relation to the matter of Hal Banks, to whom the right hon. gentleman once referred as being a demagogue in Canada. The first one- and this is one which I think ought never to have been made or entertained by a man holding so high an office as that of leader of the official opposition and who was once the prime minister of this country-was a direct accusation, without verification, against a minister of the crown to the effect that he had misled the house in making a statement. The statement referred to was that made and repeated by me, that my department or the officials under my jurisdiction had in fact requested the F.B.I. to investigate the whereabouts of Hal Banks and to report to the R.C.M.P.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I have asked myself for some moments whether it was even dignified on my part to try to give the house facts and dates in support of the denial of such an accusation. But I think that because the matter has been in the papers and has reached the news it is important that this house should ascertain when the information was requested. First I must say that on August 18, 1964, the R.C.M.P. contacted the liaison officer of the F.B.I. by telephone requesting the information which I told the house later had been requested. On the same date-
What was that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Information as to the whereabouts of Mr. Banks.
A reporter found him.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On August 18 a letter was written to the F.B.I. liaison officer by the R.C.M.P. in Ottawa. On August 25 a second letter to the same effect was written, seeking information from the F.B.I. On August 28 the F.B.I., through its liaison officer, acknowledged the last letter. Let it not be said, Mr. Chairman, that the R.C.M.P. could have gone to the United States and itself pursued there an investigation. This, as everybody knows, in accordance with international practice, would be absolutely unthinkable and unacceptable. The investigations which the
Supply-J ustice
F.B.I. intends to pursue in Canada are pursued by Canadian authorities or police, usually through the liaison officers of these police forces. There are in that way exchanges of information going on throughout the year.
Mr. Chairman, will the minister, having referred to these two letters of August 18 and 25, table the letters so we may see what he asked for?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, that is about the most appropriate question that could have been put. It is much more appropriate than were the accusations of the right hon. gentleman.
Hear, hear.

Is his conscience bothering the minister?
Som hon. Members: How about you?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You don't have a conscience.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister would answer one question at this stage.
Sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.
I do not think the minister heard me, Mr. Chairman. Would the minister answer one question now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We will see what the question is.

This question is very
simple. I have been listening to the minister with great interest but would he explain at this stage why the recognizance bond did not carry a term as a condition, taking all the circumstances into account, to the effect that Banks should stay within the jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman may be assured that if he is patient with me I will get to that point, not right away but in the course of my remarks, which I intend to make in the order I have planned.
I have here a letter dated October 5, 1964 from the deputy commissioner of the R.C.M.P., Mr. J. Lemieux, in which all the information is given and in which he refers to the correspondence to which I have made reference. I ask for permission to table that letter which is addressed to me.
The second-

Supply-Justice
Before the minister goes on, may I say that the letters I want to see are those of August 18 and 25. What do those letters contain?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Respect the rules.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If the right hon. gentleman is ready to state that he does not believe the report which has been made to me by the R.C.M. Police and in this respect insists on production of the correspondence sent and received by the R.C.M. Police-although he knows it is against the practice of the R.C.M.P. to produce copies of any correspondence-he can take the responsibility therefor and I shall make the necessary inquiry to seek their agreement for production of such copies.
Mr. Chairman, let it be made clear immediately.
Order.
The minister has referred-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.
I rise on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Leader of the Opposition on a question of privilege.
The minister said that the two letters to which I referred were sent. He now endeavours to raise an alibi and hide behind the facts.
Order.

Having referred to these letters the minister does not want to produce them, for reasons which naturally are very appealing. Why did the minister refer to these letters? He now says he does not want to produce them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I told the right hon. gentleman that, knowing what is the practice, if he wanted to take upon himself the responsibility for stating that he does not rely on the report which has been made to me by the R.C.M.P. deputy commissioner which I have just tabled and which describes the correspondence, and if he wishes to have copies of the actual correspondence tabled, I would attempt to obtain copies and file them, but under his own responsibility.

The minister has referred
to these letters. He acted on his own responsibility and we want to see what those letters contain.
Hear, hear.
We will not have this sort of evasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of all these interruptions I should like to say I wish I could use with as much authority as he often does certain of the expressions which the right hon. gentleman uses to make fellow members sit down, so that I could continue my own speech.
The second allegation which was made by the right hon. gentleman and which he insisted ought to be discussed even in the absence of the appropriate minister was to the effect that the government made a deal with Banks to allow him to leave the country smoothly thus, in his words, flouting the course of justice. This, of course, relates and could only relate to the way in which my department under my responsibility has dealt with the Banks matter following the time of his conviction, and from the moment he appealed his conviction for conspiracy in relation to the Walsh beating. I do not think anyone believes that I have to deny such imputations so that everyone will know and be confident that they do not conform to reality and are completely contrary to the truth and to the facts. However, I suppose that for the purpose of the record I owe it to this government and to this house to repeat for the purpose of the right hon. gentleman-
For the purpose of answering the labour leader who said that about you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Order. Why do you not
observe the rules?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-for the purpose of the right hon. gentleman matters which I have already put before the house which do not seem to have been well understood and therefore need to be repeated.
When Banks was convicted an application was made for his release on bail. Under section 587 of the Criminal Code he applied through his counsel to the chief justice of the court of appeals of the province of Quebec seeking the fixing of bail in his case. Counsel was instructed, and the instructions which were given to counsel representing the federal government and the counsel representing the attorney general of the province of Quebec were to oppose completely the fixing of bail so that Banks would remain within the jurisdiction of the court and attend the hearing of his appeal.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, it would be out of proportion with reality and completely illogi-

cal, once the government had attempted to take the necessary steps so that Banks might even be forced to remain in jail until his appeal had been disposed of, to say or to imply that there has been some kind of a shady deal or arrangement between the Department of Justice-because that could be the only possible department-and Banks, so as to make sure that he could leave the country very discreetly and thus flout, as has been suggested, the course of justice. I say that the very first step taken by the government of opposing any bail in the case of Banks pending his appeal completely denies any accusation or suggestion or innuendo to the effect that he would have been either pampered or assisted in leaving the jurisdiction of the courts of this country.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister allow a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sorry, but I prefer that you ask your questions later.
This is just a simple little question. Why did counsel for the crown not advise the chief justice-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.
Why did counsel not advise the chief justice that this was not an extraditable offence?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will have ample opportunity to make more of his gratuitous allegations later on.
Why did you not inform the court of appeal that it was not an extraditable offence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The attitude taken by my department and by the department of the attorney general of Quebec was taken not only in an attempt to act passively, but to make sure to maintain Banks within the confines of the court's jurisdiction. Counsel was instructed to request that if the court felt as a matter of justice it ought to fix a bail bond, the amount of the bond ought not to be less than $50,000. Again the government has acted towards Hal Banks in a way which is directly opposite to any so-called co-operation, pampering, or assistance in his flouting the course of justice in this country.
What is more serious than the accusations made by the right hon. gentleman against any member of parliament or of government is the implication on the part of one whose profession is the law that one of the greatest
Supply-J ustice
judges in this country has, in disposing of the matter of bail in the case of Banks, acted in a way which was contrary to the interests of this country. I deny that completely.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege, and throw that accusation back into the teeth of the hon. gentleman. What I said was this. This government and its counsel failed to inform that eminent judge of the fact that the charge of conspiracy was not an extraditable charge. A judge must accept what counsel places before him. I made no such allegation against the chief justice of Quebec and I want to make that very clear. This is simply a smokescreen on the part of the government to conceal its failure to give adequate information to the chief justice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Those remarks may well be a clarification of a statement made previously by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, but I do not think there is any question of privilege.
I refer to an erroneous statement about an allegation made against the chief justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a new member of parliament I have a lot to learn from the right hon. gentleman about the method of inserting remarks in the record, contrary to the rule, during the course of a statement being made by another member. I did not precipitate this discussion, Mr. Chairman, but I have attempted to make the situation clear.
The question of fixing bail under the Criminal Code and most lawyers are aware of this fact, is essentially one for the court to decide in its discretion. It is all very well for the right hon. gentleman, by hindsight, to say that not only should we have objected to any bail or bond being posted, or insisted on a very high bail, but that we should also have instructed counsel very specifically to inform the chief justice of the province that the offences were not extraditable, and that if the chief justice dared to fix bail he would have to share in the responsibility for Mr. Banks fleeing the country.

You allowed him to get
away. You answer that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
You would not like this answer twice.
I hold great respect for the chief justice of my province, who was appointed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition when he was in office, and who should perhaps be congratulated in that regard. On the occasion of that appointment I remember very clearly

Supply-Justice
writing to one of my predecessors, Hon. Davie Fulton, indicating that normally one would congratulate the appointee, but that in this regard, as a member of the bar of Quebec, I felt I should extend congratulations to the minister of justice.
It is that judge, Mr. Justice Tremblay, whose judgment is being questioned, and whose exercise of discretion is put into question by the hon. gentleman. That judge, when looking at the offences charged, knew just as well as anyone else in the courtroom that they were not extraditable. Surely he exercised his discretion in the light of all the circumstances. I wish to repeat that this decision, rendered in those circumstances was a decision which could be expected as being fair on the part of the judge who made that decision on that particular day.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would much prefer you to do so at the end of my statement.
My question relates to what the minister has just said.
Sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is not only the question in relation to the posting of bond in the case of Hal Banks which is of such great interest to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition referred specifically to the fact that in the bond there was no prohibition which would have prevented Hal Banks from leaving the country pending the proceedings. The hon. gentleman's statement would not really be believable if it were not written in Hansard at page 6000. He referred to the contents of the bond posted by Banks, without of course having taken the very ordinary precaution of looking into the matter. Sometimes when you look too far you are prevented from making a certain assertion because at that moment you know the allegation is wrong.

The hon. gentleman
looked far enough when he charged him with a non-extraditable offence.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; I have to interrupt the minister because his time has expired.
No, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed that he should continue?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank hon. gentlemen for allowing me to continue and I will not abuse the privilege. I may have another chance to rise at the end of the questions. The right hon. gentleman said that the alleged clause relating to preventing Banks from leaving the country was removed from the ordinary bond form. I showed the bond form, which I think has now been tabled, to the right hon. gentleman afterwards. I challenge anyone to tell me that there has been the slightest deletion from that bond form, let alone the deletion of a condition which would have assisted Banks in leaving the country. Just as the bond form, which we have been accused of tampering with has not in fact been tampered with, in the same manner the so-called deal which we are alleged to have made with Banks not only has not been made but it could not be made. The reference to it is contrary to all the facts as they exist. It could not possibly have been made in the light of these facts and I say that if it exists, then it exists in only one place, and that is in the imagination of the right hon. gentleman.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.

May I ask a question of the minister? He said he would answer questions at the end of his statement. Is it not the duty of crown counsel to make all the necessary representations so that the chief justice, no matter what his juridical science may be, can determine whether or not a bail bond should be granted, what the amount of it should be, and so on? Should the judge not be acquainted with all the consequences of bail, particularly in this case of Banks?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend has just stated the normal functions of the normal crown attorney. I am not going to ask him a question, but I am quite sure that throughout his life as a crown attorney, and he was a very good crown attorney, he never had occasion to tell a judge: Beware, this offence is not extraditable. This is not the normal thing to do because one expects the judge to know. I repeat, in spite of all the innuendos that are on the record, I am satisfied just as the citizens of the country are satisfied, that counsel for the crown charged with prosecuting Banks have done their duty, and only their duty.

May I direct one further question to the minister? Would he deny that as late as a month ago his parliamentary secretary, who is sitting right behind him, said to a news commentator over the radio in refer-

ence to Banks, that extradition did apply and it would be used if necessary? Will he deny that statement is on tape at the present time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps on a question of privilege I could deal with this matter. I deny I made the assertion the hon. member has just made.

Mr. Chairman, the members of the house and the public of Canada have been waiting for months for some answers to exculpate the government from this sad and sordid mess in which they have gotten themselves over Banks. Now they have been treated this afternoon to a tangled web of distortions and, in fact, fairy tales. The minister, try as he may, cannot get away from the facts which I will put straight.
Oh, oh.

You see, Mr. Chairman, how they believe in themselves; these infallible members over there believe in themselves merely because they happen to be sitting on the government side. They have not changed one iota since 1957 or prior thereto.
Before discussing the facts, Mr. Chairman, I want to state that there has been a serious point of order raised. The minister has referred to two letters, one dated August 25 and the other dated August 28, if I heard him correctly. He has referred to these letters in the debate. I believe the rules of this house require that they be tabled. I do not know what is in these letters. We have been given a partial explanation of what is in them by the minister. Since he has taken upon himself the responsibility to make a reference to those letters during the debate, then I believe the rules of this house require that they be tabled.
Why don't you steal them?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is a Liberal tactic.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, and probably we should also make it a question of order. It does seem that the Liberal members, who have been silenced by their own party, do not want to allow the opposition to speak. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that I could name the member if he wants me to, but when he states that the distinguished member now speaking should steal those letters, then he is imputing motives. I would say with greatest respect to you, Mr. Chairman, that we should ask for a little order and decorum, because if hon. members showed a little more respect perhaps parliament would 20220-560
Supply-Justice
receive more respect from the members of the press gallery and the public at large.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order please.
On a question of personal privilege, Mr. Chairman, I do not know whom the hon. member was pointing to, but I think he was pointing at me, and if he was doing so he was completely erroneous.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: If the hat fits wear it, my friend.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I would invite all members to respect the usual requirements of decorum in committee and allow the hon. member to make his speech without interruption.

This loud and raucous interference across the way really does not bother me at all, Mr. Chairman, because I have become rather used to it, particularly when the case is so strong against them, and when their own arguments are so weak that they have to pound their desks like the trained seals they are. What it amounts to-
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman-
Here is the mayor of Halifax.
He is not a trained seal.
I am not trained-
Oh, oh.

I am not trained as a member of the bar, but I know most people in Canada would like to see less of courtroom tactics and more of reason in a properly disciplined parliament, and I would hope the hon. member could proceed that way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Obviously we will not make too much progress if we keep raising questions of privilege and points of order. I would invite all members to co-operate with the Chair and allow the hon. member for Yukon to continue his remarks.
They don't like it, Mr. Chairman. They don't like being confronted with the facts.
Oh, oh.
I am sorry if I hurt the feelings of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd). He is just a seal, untrained.

On a question of personal privilege, Mr. Chairman, as I understand the rules

Supply-Justice
inherited from the members of the bar, imputations should not be made as to the conduct of any hon. member. I suggest that the hon. member address himself to the facts and not be spinning a tale, a web of intrigue which he has constructed in his own imagination.

To settle the question perhaps we could have the expert advice of the Minister of Fisheries on the subject, as to the classification of the hon. member.
As recorded at page 7960 of Hansard for September 14 the Minister of Justice, in reply to a question put to him by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, said:
I must say that although we have received lull co-operation from the United States authorities the latter have not yet been able to define the whereabouts of Mr. Banks.
There can be no question whatever but that the minister did in fact request the F.B.I. to investigate the whereabouts of Mr. Banks.
Why didn't the Leader of the Opposition admit this, then?

I will come to that. Now the press has come forth with stories purporting to emanate from sources within the F.B.I. which state the F.B.I. were not officially requested by the Canadian government to make any investigation as to the whereabouts of Mr. Banks. I believe those stories came out on Friday last.
The minister has made much about the timing of the presentation of the motion to adjourn the business of the house under standing order 26. That motion was presented at the first opportunity, and the reason it was introduced was because of a story appearing throughout the national press that a Mr. Todd, a responsible labour leader, had alleged a deal between the government of Canada and the S.I.U. with regard to the escape of Hal Banks.
That motion was presented at the first opportunity. It is regrettable that the minister and the Prime Minister were not here. Perhaps more ministers should have been here, because certainly more ministers would appear to be involved than the Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Justice in this whole shoddy affair.
Here you have two forces, the F.B.I. in the United States and the R.C.M.P. in Canada, both backed by the full resources of their two governments, both unable to trace Mr. Banks; but a Toronto Star reporter does it in two hours. Here is the F.B.I. of the United

States, who laid Dillinger and Baby Face Nelson by the heels, unable to find Banks, and it was left to a Toronto Star reporter to find him inside a two hour investigation.
What is the minister trying to tell us? What is he asking the people of Canada to believe?-that these forces of justice, great and accomplished as they are and as they have proven themselves to be, cannot find a trace of the elusive Mr. Banks, but Mr. Reguly does it in two hours, and not a very strenuous two hours at that.
Is there not justification for coming to the conclusion that there has been some sort of deal between the government and Hal Banks?
Not at all,-a lie.
This is just one fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the type of mind you have.

Mr. Chairman, I seldom take exception to any remarks made in the chamber, but one has been made just now which may find its way into Hansard and I would like the minister concerned, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who said "That is a lie" to assure me that he did not intend to impute any motives so far as I was concerned in regard to that statement.
Mr. Chairman-
Withdraw.
This is contrary to the assertions of the Minister of Justice, whose word I accept.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sure the minister and all members of the committee know well there are some words that should not be used, and certainly one of them that cannot be used is to suggest that another member has lied. Actually we had this point discussed just a couple of weeks ago in committee, and if the word has been used, as suggested by the hon. member for Yukon, and if he requests that it be withdrawn, I am sure the minister would want to explain.
No, he wants to withdraw.
Mr. Chairman, I would ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw his statement that the Minister of Justice is telling lies.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. That is not the Chair's understanding of the rules. The hon. member for Yukon, who has the floor, makes a series of assertions which are contrary to

assertions made by another member, and each, one is entitled to his own opinion, but I do not believe another member can assert one member is lying because he has contradicted a statement made by another member.
Withdraw.
I just want the minister to say he was not for a moment suggesting that I was lying. He may take exception to the statements which I made.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I assert that the hon. gentleman's statements are contrary to what I regard as the truth uttered by the Minister of Justice.
Withdraw.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the minister would want to co-operate with the committee and with the Chair, and if perhaps the word he used went beyond his thoughts I would ask him very simply to withdraw the word.
I am very happy to do so. I would not offend my hon. friend-
No conditions.
I withdraw the word.
That is better.

I seldom take exception to words used but I would not want readers of Hansard, even though they are few, to get the impression that the minister used an expression he did not want to. It is my belief that the explanation offered by the minister is more an exercise in metaphysics than it is an explanation of the law. All we want, and all we have been asking for throughout these months, are the facts. But we cannot seem to get them from the minister. He says counsel appointed by the crown opposed bail. He is a member of the bar. Having read his biographical history I am sure he has wide experience at the bar and as Minister of Justice he is gaining it now, perhaps a little more slowly here than he did while in private practice. But he knows as well as I do and as well as his colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs does, that in every recognizance crown counsel always makes certain that there is a provision in th bail bond which would prevent the accused from leaving the jurisdiction. Certainly that has been my experience in these matters against a background of some ten years prosecuting for the crown. It is not up to the judge to prepare counsel's case for him. It is up to counsel to make sure his documents are in order 20220-560J
Supply-Justice
before he puts them before the judge. Is it not natural that we who are familiar with the customary and usual practice in matters of this kind should wonder why this particular provision was left out on this occasion? Is it not natural that we should proceed from there to examine Mr. Todd's statement that there has been some sort of deal, or some connivance, between the government and Mr. Banks?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. member answer a question? Is he ready to state that the form provided by the Criminal Code in the case of a bond posted on appeal contains a clause providing for the prevention of the appellant leaving the jurisdiction? Will he not agree that in the province of Quebec, in the practice of the court of appeal, the bond which was signed by Banks was the usual and common form continuously used in that province?

The minister knows as well as I do that the procedure governing these matters is the one set forth in the Criminal Code of Canada and that it applies uniformly throughout the whole of Canada. It is no different in Quebec. It is the same as in any other province or area of Canada. The hon. gentleman knows, too, that fundamentally a recognizance is the same on appeal as it is on trial. He knows, also, that the provision as to remaining within the jurisdiction is a provision which is normally there before a person goes to trial or appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a question of privilege, that ought not to be left on the record uncontradicted. It is contrary to the practice in the province of Quebec and it is contrary to the facts.
There is no question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I recognize that. But the Chair has to listen to at least one sentence before forming an opinion. I am sure the minister realizes there is no question of privilege here. It is the minister's privilege after the hon. member has spoken, if he has an opportunity to get on record, to correct statements which he thinks are wrong. But there is no question of privilege.

Well, the minister holds his view as to the practice and I hold mine. I dare say that a great many other lawyers in the country, including prominent lawyers in Quebec who have made certain statements on this subject to the press, hold views which are entirely different from those held by the

Supply-Justice
minister. But is it any wonder that since these views are held by a number of people we should ask that there be an inquiry to determine just how deeply the government is involved in these arrangements.
The crown, said the minister, opposed the bail application. But the crown did not, according to my information, advance any argument in opposition to bail being granted. The crown did not explain-as is the duty of counsel; not of the judge or the court- that the offence with which the court was dealing was a non-extraditable offence. This is a practice so common that there should be no need for it to be repeated to members of the bar who have any knowledge whatsoever of the practice which prevails. Counsel should have told the judge that the court was dealing with an accused person who was charged with a crime which was non-extraditable.
Why were such instructions not given to the counsel retained by the minister's department? Is it any wonder that in the absence of such specific instructions people come to the conclusions that they do with respect to these arrangements with the S.I.U. and with Banks.
I wonder, too, why counsel did not acquaint the court with the record of Mr. Banks-a record which I read into Hansard during the debate on the S.I.U. bill; a record which I described as being "as long as your arm"; a record which was appended to the order in council which was signed when Banks was admitted to this country by the Liberal administration of the day. Why was not the court informed of this record, -and why were these facts not placed before the judge so that he would be better informed and able to decide whether or not there was any likelihood of Mr. Banks leaving the jurisdiction? I dare say that had this record been produced to the court then, either this particlar provision would have been inserted in his recognizance or he would not have been granted bail at all.
The facts are these. Banks was granted bail in an amount of $25,000 for a five year conviction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Those are the only facts so far.
That is a cheap price to pay to get out of the country-$5,000 a year.
Especially if you are using someone else's money.

Five thousand a year for freedom. And he was allowed-I use that word

"allowed"-to leave Canada by the fumbling and the bumbling, intentional or otherwise, of the government-a government for which the Prime Minister must take responsibility by reason of his position as head of the government, and for whose actions the Minister of Justice, together with his colleague the Minister of Labour, must also take responsibility. I do not know whether or not there are any other ministers there from Montreal. I do not know their backgrounds. But there have been some statements made with regard to radio tapes and the like which may arouse a little fear in the minds of some of those ministers and maybe in the minds of some backbenchers as well, and the thought that Banks would be a fine fellow to get out of this country.
Oh, oh.
No amount of squirming can cover up-

Would the hon. member permit a question? I understand he alleges there was some sort of deal with Banks to buy his freedom at the rate of $5,000 per annum. I take it, then, that the hon. member alleges that the chief justice was in on this deal, as he would have to be if such a deal were made.

This is a very clever but very shallow contrivance on the part of the hon. member who, I understand, had his fortunes changed by some sort of a deal in Ontario, to shift emphasis from the real issues which confront the minister and the government to some side track. All this is a red herring. The court and the judge have nothing to do but their duty, and their duty is to decide on the basis of material which is put before them by counsel, material which counsel has responsibility for producing pursuant to instructions.
What was counsel instructed to do in this case? Remain mute? To rise and say merely: "We oppose bail"? What arguments did counsel present? If none were presented, why the silence? All these interventions and smokescreens are merely designed to hide the facts. The fact is, and it is abundantly clear, that the Minister of Justice-and I do not know how many collaborators he may have had on the front benches over there- made it easy for Banks to leave this country.
Slander.

And they may have had good reason for making it easy for him to leave the country. We have seen the material that

has appeared in the column of the eminent member for Port Arthur, saying that Banks was mighty cosy with the Liberal party; saying that he referred to the Liberal party as his Ottawa bureau. No wonder then, if these allegations are correct-about which the minister says nothing, nor any other cabinet member-there is some anxiety that not only he leave the country but stay out of the country.
Who brought him in in the first place?
Illegally?

What the minister is saying in effect is that what the resources of the Canadian government, of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, of the United States government and of the federal bureau of investigation could not do over three months was done by Mr. Reguly in two hours.
At the cost of $2 for a taxi.

The minister is saying that this task of finding Mr. Banks was beyond the resources of these two governments and these law enforcement agencies. The hon. member for Renfrew South and the minister have been trying to foist the blame, deliberately, with regard to the bail application, on to the judge who presided over the court at the time the application was made. The minister had some rather critical remarks to make-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Several.

-of the motivation of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, as a member of the bar, in making this statement. I put that same charge to the minister, because I say it is pretty shoddy tactics to try to foist the blame for the government's inadequacies, deliberate or otherwise, on to a judge. It was the minister's responsibility to instruct counsel properly; it was the minister's responsibility to see that Banks came to justice; it was the minister's responsibility to see that the court was properly advised by counsel instructed by his department.

It was the court's
decision.

I hear an interjection that it was the court's decision. Naturally it was the court's decision; the court was the only agency that could make such a decision. It is a fact that it is the court's decision. But what is the court going to do if a plaintiff comes in and remains mute? Is the court going to give judgment for the plaintiff, or is
Supply-Justice
he going to decide the case on speculation which may or may not exist in his own mind? What is the court going to do with regard to a bail application if it is not told anything about the man concerning whom the application is made?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: He had not thought of that.

It is a very sad and sordid record that the government has in this regard. Its record and actions in this regard have tarnished not only the minister and the officials, whom he has not only the responsibility to direct but to guide, but they have tarnished the reputations and characters of the Prime Minister who leads this government and of the Minister of Labour; and, as I say, there may be other cabinet members involved as well. Only time will tell, and I wish Mr. Banks could tell.
He will talk, after the election.
You guys won't be talking in here after the election.
Hear, hear.
That is wishful thinking.
You speak from experience, Joe.

Mr. Chairman, in closing these few words of reply to the minister's statement I want to say this to him. I have said already that counsel, if they did not bring these matters to the attention of the court, were improperly instructed and I think there are certain motivations in this regard that should be explained by the minister or whoever did instruct those counsel. I think the minister should explain just what representations were made by counsel to the judge. These are explanations that could have been made and could have helped clarify this situation; could have helped clear the tarnished image that the government has assumed as the result of the whole sordid affair.
But instead of adopting that course the minister adopted one of attacking the right hon. Leader of the Opposition for bringing forward the motion last Monday. It is my personal view, with which undoubtedly members opposite will not agree, that this government brought Banks in, approved his actions, and he was encouraged and fraternized with by the Liberal administration right up to its defeat in 1957. The Liberals were the people that brought him in. In fact, in order to accomplish this they twisted and altered and reshaped the Immigration Act and the procedures that were operable under that act.

Supply-Justice
This is what was done in order to bring in this gentleman who is now so elusive.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member put on the record the name of the minister concerned?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Who was the minister of the day?
The former minister, Mr. Harris, was the gentleman concerned. He is the gentleman who, in accordance with my understanding of the facts-
Which is very limited.

-brought representations to bear. The hon. member for Renfrew South can check these facts if he wants to be accurate himself, and if he thinks they are wrong he can rise in his place any time and correct me.

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? I know the hon. member is very critical of the handling of Mr. Banks both before 1957 and since April, 1963. I wonder whether the hon. member could tell us in what way, between 1957 and 1963, the Banks matter was better handled than it was previously.

There is one gentleman in this house who can do that much better than I, because he was an assistant deputy minister from 1955 to 1960-and he now occupies the portfolio of Minister of Justice. At the time he was an official of the department; he was undoubtedly acquainted with all the facts; he was undoubtedly acquainted with the advice given to the government of that day-and no one can tell me that a minister of justice, unless he has very good, substantial reason, is going to act without the advice of his officials.
Would the hon. member permit another question?
Sit down.
Is the hon. member alleging that the shortcomings between 1957 and 1963-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.
Put it on the order paper.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think I should bring to the attention of the hon. member the fact that his time expired a few minutes ago. I was giving him additional minutes; but I do not think they should be used up by answering questions.
With the consent of the committee, Mr. Chairman, I might be permitted to continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think we should extend the same courtesy to the hon. gentleman as was extended to me in regard to my speech.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, we have no objection to extending the hon. member's time; but this debate is only for this afternoon and I am sure the other parties in the house have speakers they want to put forward. If the hon. member is only going to be a few minutes, that is fine; but if he is going to take some time I think hon. members from other parties should be given an opportunity to take part in this debate.

Mr. Chairman, I want to be completely co-operative in that regard. I think the matter is of sufficient concern and importance that the debate certainly should not end this afternoon and perhaps it might be carried on tomorrow; because I am going to move an amendment this afternoon in connection with these estimates and other parties in this house may wish to debate the amendment at some length.
I was speaking of the former minister, Mr. Harris, and the order in council which was signed and which admitted Mr. Banks into this country. There was appended to it a list of the convictions of Mr. Banks. Since that admission a long record of approval, of association and of amity between the Liberals and Mr. Banks has emerged. The latest episode is Mr. Bank's decamping under the noses of the government and under the noses of the most experienced law enforcement agencies.
Not only that, Mr. Chairman, but is it not curious that Mr. Banks, to use the word of the Minister of Justice, "discreetly" left the country? He discreetly left the country in a cream Cadillac with Quebec licence plates, loaded to the gunwales with all the records of the S.I.U., passing through the Canadian port of exit and the immigration port of entry to the United States.
They did not know it was he.

No, they did not know it was Mr. Banks, although he had his Cadillac on parliament hill when the demonstration took place. I am sure the minister saw it then and also a good many members of the R.C.M.P. saw it as well. I say that no party could do more for a friend. This is a friendship which is undoubtedly reciprocated by Mr. Banks.

In the good old days of Liberalism before 1957 Mr. Banks had his Ottawa bureau functioning pretty smoothly.
A government which has this sort of record by association with this gentleman, with the complete mishandling of the affair which has allowed Mr. Banks to escape Canadian justice, brings serious doubt on the capacity of the Minister of Justice to retain the portfolio he holds. In our view the minister should seriously consider submitting his resignation to the Prime Minister. Perhaps he should follow the precedent of the previous postmaster general. Before the Norris commission Banks said he got along with the Liberals; that appears in the report. He got along fine with them. In addition to letting him into the country the Liberal government even sent him to the international labour organization convention at Geneva. What a representative to represent Canada in a discussion such as that.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I am sure the hon. member does not want-or perhaps he does-to leave such a falsehood uncorrected. He said the Liberal government sent Mr. Banks. The fact is the government accepted the recommendation of the Canadian trades and labour congress, now the Canadian Labour Congress, which nominated Mr. Banks to attend the convention. That is on the record.

If this government does everything the Canadian trades and labour congress recommends, that is one matter. In 1955 the government paid Banks' way to Geneva to represent Canadian labour. He was sent over by the government because he was such a friend. I wonder at the degree of dignity and distinction with which Banks represented the Canadian government and Canadian labour while in Geneva. As late as 1963 in his report to the seafarers international union convention-this appeared in the column of the hon. member for Port Arthur-Banks attacked the Norris commission. He also attacked the previous minister of labour, now the hon. member for Ontario. He spoke very approvingly of the Liberal government, saying that the enemies of the S.I.U. were not finding the same willing ears as when the Conservative government was in power. That is what the friend of those opposite said.
He was wrong.

Now we have the interprovincial member for York-Scarborough again.
Supply-J ustice
A point of order, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is rising on a point of order.

Mr. Chairman, there is only about an hour and ten minutes left in this debate. While I think the hon. member is making a useful contribution I do not think he should be allowed to take up all the time. He has been speaking now for about 45 minutes and I think some other hon. members should also be allowed to take part. If the debate continues tomorrow he can speak again, but I do not think that the other parties should be shut out completely.

I realize the quandary of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam but I certainly shared my 30 minutes with all the hon. members who interjected and made speeches during the time I have been on my feet. I do not think I have been speaking for 30 minutes but I will take my seat and move my amendment so that the committee might study it.
May I close simply by saying this, that the Liberals caused Banks to be charged. He was convicted and they let him go, to bask in luxury on his yacht in New York, a yacht which was provided by the S.I.U. for the purpose of Mr. Banks. And let us not believe for a moment that the S.I.U. would provide such facilities for Mr. Banks if he had lost all his usefulness to that union organization.
This raises another possible suggestion here, and that is: Has the control of the S.I.U. really slipped from Banks' hands?
That is the question.

The S.I.U. do not provide these facilities for nothing. Because of the manner in which the government has failed to act on this matter; because the minister has shown a singular lack of understanding of the function with which he is charged in carrying out the responsibilities of his office; because of the degree to which the law, good order and justice in this country have been dragged in the mire by the inaction of the minister and of the government as a whole, it is both my belief and the belief of a good many of us on this side that the minister is no longer fit to hold the portfolio of Minister of Justice. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South:
That vote No. 1 of the estimates of the Department of Justice be reduced by the sum of $16,999,

Supply-Justice
That will leave by way of salary for the minister $1 per annum.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me the only possible reason for spending a day or maybe two days in debating the now famous Banks case is that there is some reason for believing Mr. Banks still exercises part or all of the control, the evil control, over the waterfront unions that he exercised for many years. It seems to me that if we believe that, and I still believe he has a great deal of influence, we ought to look at the record of what has happened.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin my remarks by stating that I am not sure how I will vote on this amendment if and when it comes to a vote. Having heard the amendment I do feel it worth while to remind members of this committee about the claims of brilliance, competence and efficiency which were made by front and backbenchers on the other side, and claims regarding how they would run the business of this country smoothly, carefully and efficiently. We all remember the broken budget, and we are now faced with this situation.
I do not blame the present minister entirely for the situation which now exists because he did to some extent inherit this situation, but I do suggest that the former government could have acted during its tenure of office and clipped Mr. Banks' wings. Certainly the ordinary people of this country who become involved in minor difficulties with the law will not have a great deal of respect for the kind of justice we have in this country, in view of the manner in which Mr. Banks has escaped the penalties imposed.
Before dealing with matters which have been discussed today, I should like to refer to two statements made by the present Minister of Justice. The other night on a television program in response to the question as to why the former Liberal government had not deported Mr. Banks, the present Minister of Justice replied that the former minister of citizenship and immigration, Mr. Harris, had accepted the advice of the immigration appeal board which heard Mr. Banks' appeal. I checked my impression in this regard very carefully with others who had heard that response. Of course that is not a true statement of the facts. The immigration appeal board, set up to hear Mr. Banks' appeal and headed by Mr. St. Onge, a senior official of the department at that time, recommended that Mr. Banks be deported. The former minister, Mr. Harris, overruled that decision of the

appeal board in the last week he held that cabinet post.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of privilege. The hon. member is referring to something which took place outside this house. While I realize it is not the practice of the hon. member to distort words and facts, and I know he did not intend to do so at this time, if he will recall correctly that interview on television he will realize I referred not to the immigration appeal board but to an inquiry made by the minister. Furthermore, one could hardly place any weight on that television interview because at least one third of my words were deleted. I do not think one should rely on that videotape program, because my remarks were taken out of their proper context.

Mr. Chairman, my relationship with the present Minister of Justice is such that I of course accept without question his statement that he did not say the former minister had accepted the recommendations of the immigration appeal board. However, I do not think it is important to my case whether the present minister made that statement or not, because the fact is that Mr. Walter Harris, at that time the minister of citizenship and immigration, did reject the recommendations of the immigration appeal board during the last week he held that cabinet position, and approved the granting of landed immigrant status to Mr. Banks. He did so I am sure with complete knowledge of a dossier on Mr. Banks, which related to Mr. Banks' life before he came to Canada.
Instead of granting that landed immigrant status to Mr. Banks by ministerial order, which is the normal practice, Mr. Walter Harris had a special order in council passed by the government, regularizing that status. In other words the whole cabinet became involved in this matter. The effect of this order in council was that Mr. Banks' landed immigration status dated back to 1952, instead of from 1954 when the case was finally disposed of by Mr. Harris. Had that not happened, I suggest it might have been easier to deport Banks when it was finally realized, belatedly, that he really ought not to have been allowed into Canada in the first place.
Mr. Chairman, one could cite incident after incident of this nature, and I am sure it is this type of thing which makes a great number of people in this country wonder about the close connections which existed between Mr. Banks and members of the former government, cabinet ministers and backbenchers, past and

present. That is the kind of common story which is circulating in every city in Canada, in newspapers, in the labour field and in the business community. I am not suggesting the minister is responsible in any way at all, but he ought to know that that is common gossip across Canada.
In discussing the prosecution of Mr. Banks several days ago the present Minister of Justice said that all the information required was available to the former government. It is not my job to defend the former government, but I think Mr. Banks' letter to the shipping companies, which came to the attention of Mr. Bernard Wilson, and through him to the former minister of labour, wherein he promised that the S.I.U. would indemnify the shipping companies if they were sued because they had not lived up to their contracts with other unions, could have been used to prosecute Mr. Banks.
The minister said that the former government did have all the information necessary to prosecute Mr. Banks. I have been informed by individuals who worked on the Banks case and know the facts, that while the Department of Justice did have a great deal of information including the testimony of Richard Greaves in 1958, and of Michael Sheehan in 1960, and knew that Walsh had been beaten in Owen Sound, it did not have evidence of any overt act in which Mr. Banks participated and for which he could be prosecuted. It did not have information or evidence linking Mr. Banks with this particular offence. In the opinion of the lawyers with whom I have discussed this situation, no charge could have been brought successfully against Mr. Banks until 1963 when the Department of Justice obtained the evidence from Mr. Bruce Smith, which he subsequently gave in court, to the effect that one of the persons present during discussions in Mr. Banks' office phoned him and asked him to establish the whereabouts of Mr. Walsh so that, as it later turned out, Mr. Walsh could be beaten. He testified further that he visited Mrs. Walsh, ascertained where her husband was in Owen Sound and communicated the information to people who went to Owen Sound and beat Walsh. Without this information the conspiracy charge certainly could not have been made to stand up. In fact, Judge Wagner devoted two pages of his judgment to Bruce Smith's testimony and to its importance.
I do not believe it is really of much value to say that the Liberal government or the Conservatives should have done it. In my
Supply-Justice
opinion, it indicates that both sides have been rather slow on the job. It has been stated in many quarters, and I think I am right in saying that at least one member of the board of maritime trustees has been quoted to this effect, that we are worrying too much about the whereabouts of Mr. Banks. This was before it was proven he was in New York. It is stated we were worrying too much about whether he had gone to-the United States or somewhere else. After all, these people said, the main thing is that Banks is gone and his position of influence in the S.I.U. has disappeared; the punishment of this Mr. Banks is not really very important. In fact, it has been said by some-people that it is a good thing to get him out of the country. Well, Mr. Chairman, one would think that Mr. Banks had been convicted and sentenced to five years in prison because he had violated a traffic law. We ought to keep in mind that Banks was sentenced to five years by Judge Wagner, who-is now the attorney general of Quebec, because the beating of Captain Walsh for which he was responsible was, and I quote from a newspaper report of Judge Wagner's charge,, a manifest act of gangsterism, agreed to, prepared, ordered, directed and supervised by Banks.
We should remember that this act of violence, of beating and gangsterism, is just one of hundreds of which Banks was accused in testimony before Mr. Justice Norris. If members of the committee are interested they can turn to the schedule prepared by Mr. Justice Norris on page 444 of the report,, and continuing for half a dozen pages, where they will find listed incident after incident,, name after name, of people who were beaten and beaten so severely that many of them were incapacitated and permanently damaged. I am not one of those people who believe that our system of justice will work if we depend only on punishment. I am one who believes in rehabilitation. Surely, if a person ever deserved to be punished for his-acts, it was Mr. Hal Banks. I suggest that when he can sit in the United States and thumb his nose at the Canadian people and Canadian justice, it is a disgrace not only to the government and the Minister of Justice but to the people of Canada as well.
I want to deal with this question of Mr. Banks and his presence in New York. It. is interesting that the Minister of Justice, day after day, and it seemed even today, talked about the alleged presence of Mr. Banks in New York. How much proof do we-

Supply-Justice
need? Does the minister have to see Mr. Banks in person before he believes that Mr. Banks is in New York? Surely that has been established. Since I came to this house I have not been known as the greatest admirer of the R.C.M.P. However, Mr. Chairman, I still retain some of the ideas that one picks up when he is young. One of the common ideas which the R.C.M.P. have not done anything to destroy-I think that is putting it mildly -is that the R.C.M.P. always gets its man. It seems to me incredible that the R.C.M.P. and their friends and colleagues in the F.B.I. of the United States, could not in fact find a man as easily identifiable as Mr. Hal Banks. I have great respect for the Minister of Justice. I do not have to look at the letters which he tabled. I take his word for the fact that he asked the R.C.M.P. to get on with the job. However, I cannot believe that the R.C.M.P. and the F.B.I. were told this was an A-l priority project. I cannot believe that if they had been told that they would not have been able to find Mr. Banks. If I believed that, Mr. Chairman, I would have serious doubts about the ability of both organizations. If I were minister of justice I would begin to think that perhaps we ought to reorganize the structure of the R.C.M.P. If they had been given instructions that this was an important matter, they could have found this man.
It was common knowledge in newspaper circles, it was common knowledge in the labour movement and I suggest, Mr. Chairman, it was common knowledge amongst R.C.M.P. officers, that it was extremely likely-I think I am speaking quite cautiously-that Mr. Banks was in New York and, in fact, was in the section of Brooklyn in which the newspaper reporter found him.
I think this man is an excellent newspaper reporter, but I, for one, do not believe he is more competent, more efficient, than the highly skilled policemen in the R.C.M.P. and F.B.I. I say it is important that we have this discussion because I believe, as do many other people who have had some acquaintance with the S.I.U. and other seamen's unions, that Mr. Banks still exerts an important influence in the S.I.U.
Prove it.
Well, Mr. Chairman, we will prove it as soon as the Minister of Labour will use the power he has to bring the board of maritime trustees before the industrial relations committee.
Hear, hear.

Day after day, week after week, members of this house have been on their feet begging the minister, entreating the minister, imploring the minister to get the board of trustees before the industrial relations committee. I wonder what else we have to do? Who are these people? Are they gods? Are they completely independent people or are they people appointed by the government of Canada under an act passed by this parliament? They should have been here long ago.
That is still not proving what you are saying.
I hope the hon. member has the courage to get up and speak, but not on my time.
I will when you are finished.
You can speak when I am finished.
That will be a real treat.
It is easy to talk.
Pay no attention; he is a blabbermouth.
I know he is a blabbermouth, and I am not worried about that. This is not the time-
I rise on a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman. There is no member in this house who is a greater blabbermouth than the hon. member who is now speaking.

That was neither a point of privilege nor a point of order, and I will give it the respect which it deserves, which is none at all.
This is not the time to discuss in detail what is going on in the S.I.U. I wish to point out to members of the committee that an election is now being held, approved and supervised by the board of maritime trustees, an election in which 10 of the 12 persons running for top offices were part of Mr. Banks' machine.
Prove it.

The hon. member does not have to believe me. He can read the report of Mr. Justice Norris where the people now running for office are listed. These are the people who will be running the organization after the election. They worked with Banks before, and we have the greatest reason to believe they will continue to work with him.
Something else has come to my attention which the Department of Labour should investigate. The board of maritime trustees ap-

proved the sending of a number of Canadian seamen to a school in New York, at which they are supposed to learn the elements of democracy. The school is called the Andrew Furuseth school and is run by the S.I.U. of North America. According to the information I have, in the interval when Mr. Banks could not be found he was acting as a teacher at this school where Canadian seamen, liberated from his domination, were being sent for instruction. I suggest that the Minister of Labour get on the job.
In a recent edition of the Canadian Sailor, published by the S.I.U. of Canada, it was announced with great fanfare that the licence division of the S.I.U. was being cut adrift from the Canadian organization and that they were going to form an independent organization. Let us just look at that and see the control which Mr. Banks may still have.
What is happening is that they have applied for a charter in the Atlantic and gulf division of the S.I.U. of North America, which is also known as the brotherhood of marine engineers. It is a constituent part of the marine engineers beneficial association of North America, and I have been told, by sources which have proven very reliable up until now, that the marine engineers beneficial association, which is dominated by Mr. Paul Hall, the president of the S.I.U. of North America, will very shortly be run by one Mr. Harold Banks, so that the licensed seamen on the great lakes of Canada will again be under the domination of Mr. Banks.
It is for reasons like that that we are interested in Mr. Banks. We are interested in what happened. We are interested in why he is not serving the sentence which Judge Wagner thought he should serve. I place no responsibility for what happened in the past on the present Minister of Justice. I merely close by saying that there are so many rumours, so many allegations, so many vicious stories being carried from one end of Canada to the other about former ministers of the Liberal government, about former members and present members of parliament from Montreal, about the amount of money which the S.I.U. of Canada gave to Liberal election campaigns while Banks was in control-there are so many of these stories that if the Minister of Justice is interested, and I think he is, in the good name of parliament, in the good name of democratic government, in the good name of his own party, and if he wants to assure the public that these stories are not true, he ought to move very quickly to appoint a judicial inquiry officer who could
Supply-Justice
look into the whole story of the S.I.U. of Canada and of Mr. Banks, and make a report to the people of Canada which would for the first time make them feel justice is indeed being done.
