At the outset I wish to say we in this party are getting a little weary of having the pot call the kettle black and vice versa. We have listened for a number of years to the charges and countercharges being hurled by the Conservative and Liberal parties across the floor of this chamber. It seems when one party is in office members of the other in opposition seem to find a number of reasons why there is some dereliction of duty, and then when they exchange positions they argue the case from the opposite viewpoint.
We think the Minister of Justice has been a little less than frank and completely open during the past few days in some of the answers he gave to questions about Hal Banks. It does not seem credible that the minister could be completely unaware of the fact that Mr. Banks had left Canada. Furthermore if the minister had been in communication with the R.C.M.P. and the F.B.I. it seems hardly credible he was not aware Mr. Banks was in New York.
It can be accepted that the minister, perhaps, could not make an official statement respecting these matters, but in many of his replies he tried to leave the impression he was not at all aware of the whereabouts of Hal Banks. In such a situation, and considering the anxiety respecting this whole matter across Canada, it would be well for the minister to be a little more frank with parliament because I am certain he has the support of all parties in it, and the support of the vast majority of Canadians in seeing to it that the kind of gangsterism which is under review is stamped out.
I am not a lawyer and am not going to get into the so-called legal procedures that it is alleged should have been taken. My information is that crown counsel did ask Judge Wagner not to grant bail at all, and this would have had the effect-
Wagner had nothing to do with it.

-of keeping Mr. Banks in custody. It seems to me this is as far as he could have gone, and that this was the maximum request that could be made. I am also informed that counsel asked that bail should not be set at less than $50,000, if bail were in fact granted. To suggest that

Supply-Justice
crown counsel was at fault when he did not remind the judge that extradition proceedings could not be taken with respect to the crime in question, does not hold a lot of weight with me because I am certain the judge must have been fully aware of that fact.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

He said he is not a
lawyer.
I just want to put this question. Mr. Justason is crown counsel for Calgary appointed by the premier of Alberta. I have been in court with him on many occasions.
What is your question?

Don't worry, you hounds who want to talk but will not make a speech. I know the hon. member is not a lawyer but does he not agree that it is the responsibility of counsel for the crown to set out the facts, and that on these facts a judge makes his decision-not on hearsay or on propaganda, which might be the kind of propaganda we read in periodicals and so on? It is on the evidence that a judge makes his decision, and without that evidence being before him how can he make a proper decision?

I will get round to the hon. member's question in a moment. The point I was trying to make is this: If the Conservative party is now trying to hang its whole case on the fact that crown counsel did not advise the judge that extradition proceedings could not be taken, it is a pretty weak case. I say this because it is evident to anyone following the case that crown counsel did in fact ask that no bail be granted at all, so Banks would have been kept in custody-
Prove it.

I cannot prove it. I have not got the transcript of evidence before me. But this has been stated in the house a number of times and I suppose it is as true as the allegation that this information was not made known to the court.
I think we must separate the two matters which are before the committee. One consideration before us this afternoon has to do with the fact that Banks was able to escape from Canada and avoid the punishment to which he was sentenced for the crime against Mr. Walsh and the beating at Owen Sound. The other matter which is of

interest to the committee and to the Canadian people is whether or not action has been taken by the government to ensure that there shall be no repetition of the incidents which have caused disruption of shipping on the great lakes-that there shall not be a perpetuation of the gangsterism which took place during Hal Banks' reign. I think we should be satisfied to some degree at least that certain action has been taken by the Department of Labour and by this house to have Banks removed from his position as president of the S.I.U. In consequence there has been reasonable peace on the great lakes during the past weeks and months.
But there are some disturbing rumours circulating, and the hon. member who spoke before me drew attention to some of them. They are to the effect that Banks may not have been removed far enough, as yet, from the labour scene. This is something which concerns all members of the house. As I said earlier, I do not intend to go over this whole question again, but I should like to review the record very briefly.
This crime of conspiracy for which Mr. Banks was convicted and sentenced related to an event which happened on August 18, 1957. If members will look at schedule 31 which was referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North they will find numerous entries there telling how people were beaten, and so on. Then, if they look to the right of the page, to the column under the heading "Action Taken", they will find time after time nothing whatever was done to deal with these offences during all those years from 1957 to 1962 when these terrible crimes were taking place. Has the law, or have procedures taken under the law, been sufficiently changed that it is no longer necessary to have an inquiry by a royal commission before anything can be done about crimes of this sort? These beatings had been taking place over many years, yet there was apparently no civilian authority with sufficient resources, strength or jurisdiction to deal with them. If this situation has not been remedied, then the House of Commons has an important task before it to see that the law is enacted and administered in such a way as to enable us to deal with these crimes without, first of all, the necessity to appoint a royal commission to bring them to light, after which there are further months of waiting before any charges are laid.
In the course of his report, Mr. Justice Norris made a number of recommendations and, as we read at page 312, he says:

Local police forces are not equipped to deal with mass action by irresponsible persons. All police forces, federal, provincial and municipal should extend their efforts to the utmost in cooperation with each other-avoiding jurisdictional jealousies-to the end that there shall be certainty in the enforcement of the law and that respect for the law will be maintained. It should not be difficult by co-operation between all police forces to reach a common understanding as to action in connection with labour disputes. It might be that police officers should have some special training on labour matters.
I know of no action which has been taken by this government or by any other jurisdiction to carry out this recommendation. As I have suggested, we had to wait from August 18, 1957, when Captain Walsh was beaten, until July 17, 1962, before anything effective was done about it. If nothing has been done to change this situation there are obviously very serious weaknesses in the enforcement of law in this country. I am more concerned that these should be corrected than I am about whether Hal Banks is brought back to Canada or not.
We know Hal Banks has been sentenced to five years. I suppose two points of view could be taken. One would be that no man should escape justice and that we should have him back and compel him to serve his five year sentence. Afterwards of course he would have paid his penalty to society and would be free to get back into the labour movement, if it would allow him to do so. The other point of view which could be taken is that as long as Banks is outside Canada with this sentence hanging over him we shall probably be rid of him for life, as far as his entry into Canada is concerned. It is not easy to decide which of these alternatives is the more desirable. But we must take some action to see that there is no likelihood of these crimes of violence recurring, and it is the responsibility of the minister to see that his department, together with all the law enforcement agencies of this country is able to deal with gangsterism of the type which has been evident over the past seven or eight years.
I do not want to be too critical of any one. As I said at the outset of my remarks I am getting a little tired of hearing the kettle call the pot black. If we turn back to the debate of October 9, 1963 when the resolution to set up the maritime trusteeship was before the house we find that some interesting remarks were made by the former minister of labour, the hon. member for Ontario, who had this to say as reported at page 3372:
Supply-Justice
The Norris commission was set up at the behest and the demand of the Canadian Labour Congress because the situation on the great lakes was intolerable. It is obvious to everyone that no government could impose such an inquiry on unions without great criticism from the labour movement in Canada unless it were done at their request. The labour movement is suspicious of moves of this kind, and unless and until they themselves feel the time is ripe for such an inquiry governments cannot move in this direction.
Mr. Chairman, I contend that if crimes are being committed, if gangsterism exists-and I presume the former minister of labour knew of the situation prior to July, 1962-a government ought to have sufficient courage to take measures to deal with this lawlessness whether or not such action is pleasing to the labour unions. If the former minister of labour expressed the attitude which motivates governments when considering whether or not action can be taken in circumstances where labour unions are involved, I can only say we must demand a complete change and the turning of a new leaf as far as law enforcement in Canada is concerned.
What concerns me, Mr. Chairman, is that apparently it was this reasoning that kept the former government from doing anything about the disruption of shipping on the great lakes, and the gangsterism that was taking place there from 1957 until 1962. That is not sufficient reason, and in my opinion it was a despicable dereliction of duty on their part.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to rise on a question of privilege. I think the hon. member who now has the floor is speaking about two different matters altogether. The first one he mentioned was the setting up of the maritime trusteeship over a union in this country. The reasons I gave were quite correct; it had nothing to do with any prosecutions or any acts of violence being committed by any member of any union. At that time there was not any evidence available with which to make prosecutions and secure convictions; there was none. There was not sufficient evidence, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North said, upon inquiry to make any prosecutions of Mr. Hal Banks with regard to any rumoured assault or battery which may have been committed at that time. It was not until the Norris commission reported that, based on that report and the advice of legal counsel from Toronto, charges could be laid.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Ontario is a little confused with regard to what I am referring to, and I will quote his words again. I was not talking about the

Supply-Justice
setting up of the maritimes trusteeship at all. I will quote his words to him:
The Norris commission was set up at the behest and the demand of the Canadian Labour Congress because the situation.. .was intolerable.
Then he went on to explain that no government, and I suppose he was referring to his own government, would have the courage -in this connection, Mr. Chairman, I will quote his exact words:
-no government could impose such an inquiry on unions without great criticism from the labour movement in Canada-
This is talking about the Norris commission and these are the words of the hon. member as reported at page 3372 of Hansard for 1963. Following that, if it had not been for that commission being set up I do not believe we would have yet reached the stage where we would have dealt with Hal Banks.
I agree-because there was no evidence before then.

The fact remains that from 1957 until 1962, while there were dozens and dozens of assaults and crimes of all kinds committed on the lakefront and in the maritime areas in general, nothing was done. Even up until that time it is the statement of the former minister that until the Canadian Labour Congress was ready to accept this kind of inquiry-that is, the Norris inquiry- he did not have the courage to even initiate an inquiry.
We have the Norris recommendations. Some of them have been acted on; some of them have not. But if we are again moving into a situation where Hal Banks-and he is not the only one-is in fact going to have a great deal of influence and is going to be in a position where he can continue this kind of gangsterism, then we have the responsibility to change the law in some respects. 1 might also point out that one or two other things have not been taken care of by the present government, because at page 311 of his report Mr. Justice Norris says this:
I recommend that special counsel be appointed to review all the facts available with a view to ascertaining whether charges should be laid in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario against Banks, McLaughlin and others-
That has not been done up to this stage either. Banks has been charged, convicted and sentenced. McLaughlin, to my knowledge, has not been charged, and the others to whom Mr. Justice Norris referred have not been charged. We would like the minister to take the kind of action that will make it impossible for Banks, McLaughlin and the others

to whom Mr. Justice Norris referred to perpetuate their control over the S.I.U. and also their being in a position to engage in crimes of conspiracy, and so on.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I just want to say again that we should have united action in this matter from all parties in the house. I was rather proud of the House of Commons the day we passed the maritime trusteeship bill because there was almost unanimity that here was a situation that was intolerable so far as we were concerned, and we were prepared to deal with it on that basis, in spite of demonstrations that were taking place on the lawn outside the House of Commons and in spite of some fears with regard to what the labour unions in Canada might think of us. This is not a matter of whether or not you are in favour of labour unions and the work they do; it is a matter of whether or not you are in favour of enforcing the law and whether or not you are in favour of protecting people against this kind of gangster.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would like to impress upon the Minister of Justice that we think some progress has been made in cleaning up this mess, but that there is a great deal of work to be done. We would therefore urge him to get on with it as soon as possible and take into account some of the other recommendations Mr. Justice Norris has made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to follow on right after the hon. member for Medicine Hat, in view of the references he made to the observations and recommendations of Mr. Justice Norris at page 311 of his report with respect to possible prosecutions. I think, in view of statements attributed to Mr. James Todd of the Canadian maritime union and repeated in this house by the Leader of the Opposition last Monday, it is desirable to set clear the record in respect of the prosecutions and action taken by the government following upon those recommendations.
The hon. member read part of the middle paragraph appearing at page 311 of Mr. Justice Norris' report and referred to the fact that Mr. Justice Norris recommended that special counsel should be appointed to look into the facts referred to and the evidence of assaults and other violence referred to by Mr. Justice Norris. Perhaps I might go on and read from page 311 where Mr. Justice Norris says:
In my opinion, the available evidence is such that the actions of these persons, upon proof of the facts,-

I would lay stress upon those words:
-are outside the exemptions provided in sections 409-411 of the Criminal Code of Canada. Counsel should also consider the evidence to ascertain whether charges should be laid against Banks and others for conspiracy to commit indictable offences, particularly in connection with acts of violence such as the beatings of Walsh and others. Consideration should also be given to prosecuting Banks and others under section 4, subsection 4, of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act on the grounds of intimidation and coercion.
I would like to refer to the fact that following immediately upon this recommendation the former minister of justice, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, announced to this house on July 18, 1963, that two eminent counsel-and if I may say so, perhaps the two most eminent counsel in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec-had been retained by the government for the purpose of examining those charges. I would refer to the fact that the crown retained Mr. John J. Robinette, Q.C., of Toronto, a former treasurer of the Law Society of Upper Canada and a man who occupies perhaps a pre-eminent position at the common law bar. The crown also retained the leader of the Quebec bar, Mr. Jean Martineau, Q.C., who was then the batonnier of the bar of Montreal. These two gentlemen were immediately retained for the purpose of examining the evidence given by various parties in respect of offences and other matters to the Norris commission, and they were also retained to advise the R.C.M.P. on additional investigations that should be carried out.
Following on this appointment the two counsel considered at once not only the broad recommendations but some other factual and notorious matters which had come to the attention of the crown in respect to the activities of Banks. I observe that the special crown counsel specifically recommended that conspiracy charges should be laid not only against Banks but also against Richardson and Carsh, the two other accused in connection with the Walsh beating. The conspiracy charges were laid on October 23 and on November 5 Banks was arrested. Subsequent to this, on May 1, 1964, Banks was convicted of these charges.
Let me also point out that the crown counsel, after very extensive investigations of the evidence and other matters, arrived at the conclusion, on the basis of further investigation by the R.C.M.P., that charges should be laid against Banks in connection with the beating of one Richard Greaves, and in due course these charges were laid against Banks and others for conspiring to injure and
Supply-Justice
commit assault upon Greaves. These charges have yet to come up for trial.
I would also point out that extensive examination was made by counsel into evidence based on the various financial records and accounts of the misuse of funds which Mr. Justice Norris had referred to in the course of his report. It was the opinion of the crown counsel that there was not sufficient evidence adduced either from the investigations or before the Norris commission, or from the report of Mr. Justice Norris himself, to justify prosecution either for theft or embezzlement. Let me repeat for the benefit of the committee that this was the recommendation of the two most eminent members of the bar in Ontario and Quebec.
At the same time the two counsel were also invited by the government to consider charges on a broader basis against Banks and his union associates. In the course of the recommendations of Mr. Justice Norris he suggested that a general charge might be laid against Banks and others with regard to the pattern of beatings and intimidations which is so graphically set out in schedule 31 to the Norris report. It was the conclusion of the counsel in this particular respect that once again there was insufficient evidence available to support a general charge of that kind.
The two counsel were specifically invited as part of their responsibilities to consider the incidents arising out of the affairs which came very close to us here, the appearance of the seamen on parliament hill. As a result of their investigations they recommended that a charge be laid against Banks, McLaughlin and others in respect of the walk-off from the ships. That particular charge comes up for preliminary hearing in a matter of a few days.
What I should point out, and what perhaps is not evident to members of the committee who are not members of the legal profession, is that none of the charges which have been laid and which were laid on the recommendation of counsel were in respect of extraditable offences. In fact, none of the specific charges referred to by Mr. Justice Norris in the passage to which I have just referred were in respect of extraditable offences. The only charges which seemed to offer any reasonable prospect of successful prosecution were in respect of theft and embezzlement; and it was the specific finding of counsel that no effective charges could be laid and they recommended against such charges being laid. These were the only possible charges which in fact would involve extraditable offences.

Supply-Justice
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would wish to counter most strenuously the assertion made by Mr. James Todd of the Canadian maritime union that the crown only chose those charges which they knew were not extraditable. The crown chose those charges upon which there was available evidence and upon which, on the advice of very eminent counsel, there would seem to be reasonable prospect of successful prosecution; and I would point out that the crown, on the basis of the advice and assistance of those counsel, have had particular success in several of those prosecutions. Therefore I would say that the charges made by Mr. Todd and which were repeated in the house by the right hon. gentleman in support of the application he made to move the adjournment of the house were completely unfounded. They appear to have been made on a misunderstanding by Mr. Todd of the actual terms of the Norris report, and they were evidently made by Mr. Todd without any knowledge or realization at all of the available grounds for prosecution under the Norris report.
I think it should be amply clear to all, Mr. Chairman, that the crown should not be laying charges where there is no evidence to support them. Widespread investigation by Mr. Justice Norris, with the assistance of many others, including people in the shipping industry and in the unions, was made concerning the events surrounding the operations of the union, but these investigations failed to disclose any evidence on which to found a charge. I think this committee should summarily reject the innuendo involved in Mr. Todd's statement that only special charges were laid.
That was the commissioner's job.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let me point out to the hon. member that under the order in council appointing the commissioner the commissioner was to make widespread investigation into all the operations surrounding the St. Lawrence and great lakes seaways, including the operations of the S.I.U. and the activities of Mr. Banks. It is in respect of these that Mr. James Todd suggested there was a selective laying of charges. I say to the hon. members of this committee and to Mr. Todd that that is a completely false allegation and one which no responsible labour leader could in all conscience make.
How many labour leaders are responsible?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, I will not develop the suggestion of the hon. member for Bow River.
This afternoon we heard from the hon. member for Yukon, who made what seemed to me a large number of innuendos about people on this side of the house and about the manner in which this case has been handled. I hesitate not one moment to reject them as completely untrue and as being a completely unfair and twisted statement of what has taken place on this matter. Let me refer in particular to the point the hon. member made about the statement made earlier by the Minister of Justice. The hon. member suggested that in some way it was a neglect of duty on the part of the minister that there was no provision in the bail bond recognizance that the accused should not leave the jurisdiction. I have had occasion to speak previously in this regard. I have also had occasion to speak to it in response to the Leader of the Opposition, on which occasion he read into the record the wrong form used in these cases. I would point out to the hon. member, as I pointed out to him then, that it is not true to say that there is any customary form under the Criminal Code which is used for this purpose on appeals and which includes such provision in a bail bond recognizance.
I would also point out that whatever may be the practice in other provinces in this country, and whatever may be the practice in these matters as opposed to the substantive law, the practice of the courts varies from province to province. It is not true to say that under the rules of the courts of the province of Quebec it is customary to have any such form of recognizance at all. I would point out-and here I am really retailing the opinion of the eminent counsel who have been advising the crown-that I am advised that it is not and has never been the customary practice in the courts of the province of Quebec to include any such provision in a bail bond such as that referred to by the hon. gentleman.
We have heard a great many wild and unfounded statements both inside and outside the house retailed by members of the house and also members of the press. One of them which I would reject most strenuously, and one of the imputations made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, is that in some way the R.C.M.P. should assume the responsibility for the fact that the federal bureau of investigation of the United States were unable to locate Hal Banks. I point out,

as the minister pointed out in his introductory remarks, that it would not, either in accordance with international law or in accordance with sound practice, be proper for the R.C.M.P. to engage in investigations with respect to a Canadian citizen in a foreign country, and more particularly in the United States. One can imagine the storm that would be raised in this house if the reverse situation took place, and the F.B.I. carried on such an investigation in Canada.
Is the F.B.I. that bad?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That may be a good question, but I do not think it is fair to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, after following their instructions and requesting the assistance of the federal bureau of investigation in this regard, that they should be required to bear the onus, which some hon. members would like to put on them, for the non-discovery of Banks. As the letter tabled by the minister very aptly discloses, the R.C.M.P. were instructed, and followed up those instructions, to request the assistance of the F.B.I. in locating Banks. If the F.B.I. did not or could not do so, I do not think the responsibility should be placed in any way on the R.C.M.P. I think I may be joined by many members of this house in saying that we resent the imputation of incompetence, which has been made by some hon. members opposite, in respect of the R.C.M.P.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that we should perhaps bear in mind just exactly what the situation was at the conclusion of the former government's tenure in office, or even before the publication of the Norris report and the commencement of action by this government. We should bear in mind that Mr. Banks was in strong control of the seafarers international union, free of any kind of prosecution for the various offences that had been taking place during a period of five years of a reign of terror on the Canadian great lakes. No action was taken at that time by the government then in power to prevent him from carrying on with those particular activities.
Mr. Chairman, it might be useful to make some reference to schedule 31 of the Norris report, and more particularly to the sad category of assaults and other violence which took place during the course of office of the government of hon. gentlemen opposite. I refer particularly to schedule 31 at page 444 and following of the Norris report, which lists incidents of assaults, beatings and terrorism, commencing with the beating of Captain Walsh on August 18, 1957, and further inci-
Supply-J ustice
dents on November 6, 1959, January 30, 1960, August 1961, October 31, 1961, April 26, 1962, April 28, 1962, April 29, 1962 and so on, page after page. These incidents include intimidations, beatings, telephone threats and har-assments. What did hon. gentlemen opposite do about that situation then? The response of the former minister of justice was just a shrug of the shoulders and the statement that they could not do anything about it because it was beyond federal jurisdiction.
I should like to refer hon. members to schedule 15 of the Norris report and appendices at page 407, which is a letter from Mr. E. D. Fulton, the then minister of justice, which in part reads as follows:
As I explained to you in my previous letter, the constitutional and legal position is clear that the primary responsibility for the maintenance of law and order and the protection of property rests with provincial authorities.
Who said that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is what Mr. Fulton said. He then continued in this letter as follows:
The acts complained of are in the nature of offences against the Criminal Code and any investigations and prosecutions in respect thereof are matters to be undertaken by local police authorities and provincial crown attorneys.
Who drafted the letter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It does not matter who drafted the letter. Who signed the letter?
This is a new Tory theory of constitutional responsibility in Canada, in which they take no responsibility. This is a new theory not of constitutional responsibility but of constitutional irresponsibility.
May I recall, Mr. Chairman, that when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office they were quick to take the credit for anything that took place, such as for the sale of wheat to China. In that regard the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, at great expense to the taxpayers, flew out to Hong Kong after the contract was negotiated, for the purpose of pushing the civil servants into the background and taking credit. However, when it comes to a question of accepting responsibility, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has said, "No, we are not responsible for that letter, just because my colleague signed it".
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the hon. member a question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make it clear that I am not yielding the floor, but simply allowing a question.

Supply-Justice

I cannot understand how you nan accuse the Conservative government of having responsibility. If that is the case, why do you not read into the record what Hal Banks himself said about the Liberal party, the Conservative party and other parties?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member for Port Arthur appears to be very much persuaded by statements made by Mr. Hal Banks. He is the man he would rely upon in this regard. At page 249 of the Norris report Mr. Justice Norris has this to say about that supporter of the hon. member's case:
Banks is capable, decisive, egocentric, intolerant and ruthless. He is of the stuff of the Capones and the Hoffas of whom the dictators throughout history, from the earliest times to the totalitarians, Hitler and Stalin, are prototypes.-In his mouth, the use of the word ''democracy'' is sheer blasphemy. For him the "big lie" and the failure to remember are ever-ready weapons and shields.
That is the witness the hon. member for Port Arthur calls upon to support his case.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I only have a few minutes left and I think I should be allowed to complete my remarks.
Six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please.
Progress reported.

This afternoon during the proceedings of the committee of supply the Minister of Justice presented a letter for tabling. With the permission of the house, the Chair will regularize the proceedings by having the letter tabled now. Is it agreed that the letter be now tabled?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, during the debate this afternoon I raised a further question concerning the minister's reference to letters of August 15 and August 28, and I suggested that by the rules of the house he is obliged to table them also. I am wondering whether Your Honour will now make a ruling.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I said that I would not affront the R.C.M.P. Perhaps I did not use exactly those words, but I said I would not accept the implication that their report should not be accepted, and then asked for leave to table that report which you now have in your hand, and which is in fact a letter from the R.C.M.P. to me.

I also said I would attempt to obtain leave to produce copies of the two letters referred to in this report, if my hon. friends on the other side of this house would accept the responsibility for insisting that I do so. I am not asking for the tabling of them.
Speaking to the point of order, I may say that the rules of the house are specific. The minister made reference to the letters and by reason of that fact I believe he is required to table them.

My intention has been drawn to standing order 59, paragraph 4, which reads:
The chairman shall maintain order in the committees of the whole house, deciding all questions of order subject to an appeal to the house; but disorder in a committee can only be censured by the house, on receiving a report thereof.
May I ask what Your Honour intends to do concerning the question of order relating to the tabling of the two letters referred to by the Minister of Justice on his responsibility?
This is a matter for the committee. I read paragraph 4 of the standing order to indicate this. It is now after six o'clock, and I intend to leave the chair.
The Minister of Justice hides again.

subtopic: FOURTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
FOURTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: If I could have unanimous consent to revert to presenting reports, I should like to present the fourteenth report of the special committee on procedure and organization.

subtopic: FOURTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder if, for the convenience of hon. members, we could ascertain the business of tomorrow? The Acting Prime Minister promised we would have the estimates of the Department of Justice up on Thursday, and that was confirmed by Mr. Speaker himself when this was discussed on Monday. I presume we shall continue with this debate tomorrow.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said, when I was asked the other day, the Minister of Justice would introduce his estimates for the purpose of this particular item not later than Thursday; that is what I said.
No, no.
My hon. friend and I do not quarrel about things like this. Hansard has what I said.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
When we looked at Hansard,
I almost raised a point of privilege to inquire whether or not Hansard had been altered. The statement was on Thursday, and Mr. Speaker, as reported on page 8725 of Hansard said:
I am informed today that the estimates of the Minister of Justice will be before the house on Thursday-
This was the understanding in the house at the time.

My hon. friend does not want to create a situation which does not exist. Later in the afternoon I went to the hon. member for Bow River, the Leader of the Opposition was not here, and told him about this. He did not have any authority to act for the Leader of the Opposition, but would take note of it. There is nothing out of the way in the situation.

So there will be no
mistake about what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said the other day, he said this matter would come up on Thursday; that is what he said.

As the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentions, he did speak to me. He said it might not be possible Thursday and he would bring it up Wednesday. I said Wednesday was a short day and I had no authority to speak for the party. He said well, likely it could go on on Friday. The fact is we have been cut off, silenced by choosing Wednesday.
Well, I do not want to intervene. Surely, the parties can get together and reach an agreement on this matter.

Mr. Speaker, it is true
that the minister for external affairs (Mr. Martin) stated a few days ago that we would discuss on Thursday the Hal Banks affair.
Tonight we did not reach a definite conclusion, and that is what Her Majesty's loyal opposition wishes us to know. Then, when can we further discuss the case of that individual? That is what I would like to find out from the Minister of Justice or the minister for external affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, knowing my hon. friend, the member for Villeneuve, I am
Business of the House
convinced that, were he aware of what I will say in a few seconds, he would not continue this discussion in the absence of the minister, particularly after the charges made by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
It is evident that, if such a statement was made by the Secretary of State for External' Affairs, there was a misunderstanding, not exactly between us, but there was a lack of precision in stating the business of the house.
Tomorrow I shall be away from Ottawa on official business.
Not political business?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, not political business. [Text]
Will the minister be available on Friday?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will be available on Friday. I will try to tell the right hon. gentleman what he is doing when he is putting that question. It would be so easy now for us to have the balance of the debate on the balance of my estimates.
When?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not plan to be here on Friday, but I will be here. There was a serious reason for me not to be here.
You are the house leader; why should you not be here?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will announce the government business that has been planned. I could undertake to bring my estimates next Wednesday if it is agreeable to the house.
No, no.

I rise on a point of order. If there is no more co-operation than that on the part of the government, I will not argue it at all. We are prepared to take it on Friday because he is going to be away tomorrow. There is a motion before the house which deserves the earliest consideration of the house, and Friday is that day. It does not in any way incommode the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman has lost his sense of proportion, his sense of relativity and his sense of distinction between the time when he was prime minister and the time he is Leader of the Opposition.
